Revised twice more the same day per Dr. Paul's direct feedback: (1) simplified the language for a non-technical (CMO-level) reader and spelled out every acronym in parentheses on first use — jargon removed or replaced: 'CI pipeline/lint gate' (dropped), 'CSS custom properties' (-> 'shared style file'), 'token drift'/'structural drift' (-> 'small style details' / 'bigger mistakes'), 'byte-identical' (-> 'word for word'), 'diff' (-> 'results'), 'on its own recognizance' (dropped); (2) reframed the hook to explicitly chain off Experiment 1's finding — the real question isn't an abstract 'can documentation heal itself,' it's 'Experiment 1 showed AI can replace the CMS; a CMS also normally keeps a site consistent — what's doing that job now that it's gone?' page.title: If AI Replaced the CMS, What Stops the Site From Drifting? | Lab | Dr. Paul Ress, DBA
page.meta_description: Experiment 2: Experiment 1 found AI can replace a content management system (CMS). This one asks what replaces the job the CMS was quietly doing — keeping the site consistent — and whether a design rulebook and a simple automatic checklist can fill that gap.
page.social_description: Experiment 2: Once AI replaced the CMS, Dr. Paul tested whether a design rulebook could keep the site from drifting.

h1: If AI replaced the CMS, what stops the site from drifting?
lede: Experiment 1 found that AI can replace a content management system (CMS). But a CMS quietly does something else too: it keeps a site consistent, page after page, without anyone having to think about it. Once AI took over and the CMS was gone, Dr. Paul tested whether a written design rulebook, plus a simple automatic checklist, could do that job instead.
hypothesis_text: A design rulebook, backed by a simple automatic check, can keep an AI-built website consistent — doing the job a CMS normally does, without a CMS in place.
finding_text: Some of the job, yes. Small style details — colors, spacing, fonts — update everywhere at once, because every page pulls them from one shared file, so that part fixes itself. But the CMS's other job, catching bigger mistakes before they ship, doesn't happen on its own. Someone, or something, still has to notice those on purpose.
limitations_text: Some mistakes were caught on this site — not a controlled study, and not enough to prove this works everywhere. But it worked to an extent.

flow_steps.title: Launch
flow_steps.body: A new page or change — often drafted by AI — goes live. Nothing else automatically stops a mistake from shipping.

experiment_lede: The artifact isn’t a writeup — it’s the automatic checklist itself (scripts/audit-site.py), watching over the same AI-built site from Experiment 1, plus the two real mistakes it’s already helped catch, described in the design system’s own rules.
human_handled: Deciding what counts as a mistake
stats_line: 9 pages checked · 2 real mistakes caught · a clean re-check the day this page went live
worked_text: The automatic checklist reliably catches the bigger mistakes — it's flagged nothing since, and stayed clean even while this very page was being built.
constraint_text: It can't catch mistakes in the writing itself — repeated wording, outdated phrasing, a wrong reference. That needed a separate tool built just for text.
finding_statement:
Replacing the CMS didn’t remove the job.
It just left it unassigned.
finding_support: Small style details fix themselves automatically — colors, spacing, and fonts update everywhere at once, because every page pulls them from the same shared style file.
finding_support_2: Bigger mistakes aren’t automatic — a leftover sentence sat in one page’s footer until a person noticed it. That’s exactly why an automatic checklist now runs before every page goes live, instead of relying on memory.
implication_text: Swapping AI in for a CMS doesn’t just remove a tool — it removes whatever that tool was quietly enforcing. Something has to pick that job back up, on purpose.
takeaway_text: If you replace the CMS, replace what it was enforcing too. A design rulebook only works if something keeps checking it against what actually went live.
